rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqā allows the comparison particle kāf to attach to “We gave you,” with the sense of giving the seven oft-repeated verses as revelation like the earlier revelation.
rows.anchor: أما الوجه الأول وهو تعلق كما بآتيناك فذكره أبو البقاء على تقدير

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد والعوفي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Mujahid, also transmitted by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, identify the dividers as the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله إن المقتسمين هم أهل الكتاب فهو قول الحسن ومجاهد ورواه العوفي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, says they divided the Qur’an among themselves.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله اقتسموا القرآن فهو قول ابن عباس فيما رواه عنه سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says they divided it by assigning some passages to al-Baqara, some to Al Imran, and so on.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله اقتسموا فقال بعضهم سورة البقرة وبعضهم سورة آل عمران إلخ فقاله عكرمة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the dividers as named Quraysh mockers who assigned different Qur’anic creatures to themselves in ridicule; God destroyed them all.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي هم الأسود بن عبد المطلب والأسود بن عبد يغوث والوليد والعاصي والحرث بن قيس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says “the Qur’an” here refers to what the People of the Book read from their own scriptures.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله إن القرآن عبارة عما يقرأونه من كتبهم إلى آخره فقاله مجاهد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects making “those who made the Qur’an into fragments” an object of “the warner”: its adjective intervenes, which Basran grammar disallows, though Kufans allow it.
rows.anchor: فلا يجوز أن يكون منصوبا بالنذير كما ذكر لأنه موصوف بالمبين ولا يجوز أن يعمل إذا وصف قبل ذكر المعمول على مذهب البصريين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies them as people who split the Qur’an into magic, poetry, and legends, but his report substitutes soothsaying for poetry.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله الذين يجزؤون القرآن إلى سحر وشعر وأساطير فمروي عن قتادة إلا أنه قال بدل شعر كهانة.

rows.speaker: السائب
rows.claim: Al-Saʾib identifies the dividers as a Meccan coalition led by al-Walid, who assigned accusations of soothsaying, sorcery, poetry, or madness; they agreed to deny the Messenger, and all were destroyed.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله الذين اقتسموا مداخل مكة فهو قول السائب

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن زيد
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Zayd says the dividers were those who agreed to spend the night plotting against Salih.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله إنهم الذين تقاسموا أن يبيتوا صالحا فقول عبد الله بن زيد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects the preceding Ibn ʿAtiyya analysis because the comparison belongs to God’s speech; a defense instead attaches it to an understood warning of like punishment.
rows.anchor: أما قوله وهو عندي غير صحيح إلى آخره فقد استعذر بعضهم عن ذلك فقال الكاف متعلقة بمحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says the wording of Ibn ʿAtiyya’s following proposal is garbled, probably by a copyist, and suggests it may have read that God sent down to Muhammad as to them.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله والذي أقول في هذا المعنى إلى آخره فكلام مثبج ولعله من الناسخ ولعله أن يكون وأنزلنا عليك كما أنزلنا عليهم.

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqā offers readings in which the comparison describes respite followed by punishment, or a warning like the one sent down.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء وقيل التقدير متعناهم تمتيعا كما أنزلنا والمعنى متعنا بعضهم كما عذبنا بعضهم.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another proposed reading treats the kāf as extra, leaving “I am the clear warner of what We sent down on the dividers.”
rows.anchor: وقيل الكاف زائدة التقدير أنا النذير المبين ما أنزلنا على المقتسمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers that the Prophet be told to warn believers and unbelievers alike, with kāf modifying an understood “a saying”: the same warning applies to both groups.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر لي أنه تعالى لما أمره بأن لا يحزن على من لم يؤمن وأمره بخفض جناحه للمؤمنين أمره أن يعلم المؤمنين وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s warning to believers remains in force even after being told to lower his wing to them; he is to warn them just as he warns the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: فالقول للمؤمنين في النذارة كالقول للكفار المقتسمين لئلا يظن إنذارك للكفار مخالف لإنذار المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those” most naturally modifies “the dividers”; it could instead predicate an omitted subject or stand in the accusative as a rebuke.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الذين صفة للمقتسمين وجوزوا أن يكون خبر مبتدأ محذوف ويجوز أن ينتصب على الذم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also allows “those” to be construed as the object of “the warner.”
rows.anchor: وتقدم تجويز الزمخشري له أن يكون مفعولا بالنذير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God swears by His own being and lordship, joining the Messenger to the oath as an honor.
rows.anchor: فوربك أقسم تعالى بذاته وربوبيته مضافا إلى رسوله على جهة التشريف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We shall question them” most likely refers to the dividers, as a threat of rebuking interrogation.
rows.anchor: والضمير في لنسألنهم يظهر عوده على المقتسمين وهو وعيده من سؤال تقريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the pronoun to include everyone, believers and unbelievers, since both groups were mentioned and the questioning is universal.
rows.anchor: ويقال إنه يعود على الجميع من كافر ومؤمن إذ قد تقدم ذكرهما والسؤال عام للخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about what they did may be a metonym for recompense, and their deeds means all their actions.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون السؤال كناية عن الجزاء وعن ما كانوا يعملون عام في جميع الأعمال.

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya says people will be asked what they worshipped and how they answered the messengers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية يسأل العباد عن حالتين عن ما كانوا يعبدون وعن ما أجابوا المرسلين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they will be asked, “Why did you do that?”
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس يقال لهم لم عملتم كذا؟

rows.speaker: أنس وابن عمر ومجاهد
rows.claim: Anas, Ibn Umar, and Mujahid say the questioning concerns the testimony “there is no god but God.”
rows.anchor: قال أنس وابن عمر ومجاهد السؤال عن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: الزهراوي عن النبي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawi also transmits this interpretation from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وذكره الزهراوي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If that report is established, the question concerns fulfilling the testimony sincerely; Hasan says faith is what settles in hearts and deeds confirm, not outward display or wishful thinking.
rows.anchor: وإذا ثبت ذلك فيكون المعنى عن الوفاء بلا إله إلا الله والصدق لمقالها كما قال الحسن ليس الإيمان بالتحلي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses “proclaim openly” as carrying out what the Prophet is commanded.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس فاصدع بما تؤمر امض به.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says it means speak aloud and make the message clear, deriving the expression from dawn breaking.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي اجهر به وأظهره من الصديع وهو الفجر

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses ṣadīʿ for the bright blaze on a horse’s forehead, illustrating the word’s dawn-related sense.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: كأن بياض غرته صديع

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi glosses the command as speaking what one is commanded to say.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي تكلم بما تؤمر.

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says it means informing people by conveying the message.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد أعلم بالتبليغ.

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Bahr says to state the call to faith plainly to them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بحر جرد لهم القول في الدعاء إلى الإيمان.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة عن رؤبة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda, citing Ruʾba, calls the phrase especially obscure: mā is relative, with an omitted second object and deleted preposition from “what you are commanded to do.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة عن رؤبة ما في القرآن أغرب من قوله فاصدع بما تؤمر وما في بما بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats mā as relative and reconstructs “proclaim what you are commanded to proclaim,” with a noun, preposition, and pronoun omitted.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش ما موصولة والتقدير فاصدع بما تؤمر بصدعه فحذف المضاف ثم الجار ثم الضمير.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows mā to be a verbal noun, meaning “by your being commanded”; Abu Hayyan rejects this analysis because the passive verbal noun construction is invalid.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن تكون ما مصدرية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the instruction to turn away from the polytheists belongs to the truce verses later abrogated by the sword verse.
rows.anchor: وأعرض عن المشركين من آيات المهادنات التي نسختها آية السيف قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God spared the Prophet the mockers through afflictions that struck them without his effort or hardship.
rows.anchor: ثم أخبره تعالى أنه كفاه المستهزئين بمصائب أصابتهم لم يسع فيها الرسول ولا تكلف لها مشقة.

rows.speaker: عروة وابن جبير
rows.claim: Urwa and Ibn Jubayr name the mockers as al-Walid, al-Asi, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Abu Zamʿa, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, and al-Harith ibn al-Talātala, though the report says five.
rows.anchor: قال عروة وابن جبير هم خمسة: الوليد بن المغيرة والعاصي بن وائل والأسود بن المطلب

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الهذلي عن الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri reconciles Ibn Jubayr’s al-Harith ibn ʿAyṭala and Ikrima’s al-Harith ibn Qays as one man, ʿAyṭala son of Qays.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الهذلي قلت للزهري إن ابن جبير وعكرمة اختلفا في رجل من المستهزئين

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi’s inclusion of Hibar ibn al-Aswad among the mockers is mistaken: Hibar converted at the conquest and moved to Medina.
rows.anchor: وذكر الشعبي في المستهزئين هبار بن الأسود وذلك وهم لأن هبارا أسلم يوم الفتح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas counts eight mockers; one transmission substitutes ʿAdi ibn Qays for al-Harith ibn Qays.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أن المستهزئين كانوا ثمانية وفي رواية مكان الحرث بن قيس عدي بن قيس.

rows.speaker: الشعبي وابن أبي بزة
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi and Ibn Abi Bazza count seven, naming al-Walid, al-Harith ibn ʿAdi, the two al-Aswads, al-Athram, and the two sons of al-Harith ibn al-Sibaq.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي وابن أبي بزة كانوا سبعة فذكر الوليد والحرث بن عدي والأسودين والأثرم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil gives the same list but replaces al-Harith ibn ʿAdi with al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال مقاتل إلا أنه قال مكان الحرث بن عدي الحرث بن قيس السهمي

rows.speaker: المفسرون والمؤرخون
rows.claim: Exegetes and historians say Gabriel told the Prophet he had been ordered to deal with the mockers, then indicated them individually.
rows.anchor: وذكر المفسرون والمؤرخون أن جبريل عليه السلام قال لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أمرت أن أكفيكهم

rows.speaker: المفسرون والمؤرخون
rows.claim: Gabriel indicated al-Walid; an arrow snagged his garment, and when pride kept him from bending to remove it, it struck a vein in his heel.
rows.anchor: فمر بنبال فتعلق بثوبه فمنعه الكبر أن يطامن لنزعه فأصاب عرقا في عقبه.

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقسم
rows.claim: Qatada and Miqsam say the arrow severed al-Walid’s al-akḥal vein, killing him.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة ومقسم وهو الأكحل فقطعه فمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel’s gesture at al-Asi’s sole led to a thorn entering it; another account says a snake caused his leg to swell like a millstone until he died.
rows.anchor: وأومأ إلى أخمص العاصي فدخلت فيه شوكة. وقيل ضربته حية فانتفخت رجله حتى صارت كالرحى ومات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel’s gesture at al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib’s eyes was followed by his blindness and death.
rows.anchor: وأومأ إلى عيني الأسود بن المطلب فعمي وهلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel’s gesture at al-Harith ibn Qays’s nose was followed by pus flowing from it and his death; another account says a poison wind blackened him, his family rejected him, and he died wandering Mecca.
rows.anchor: وأشار إلى أنف الحرث بن قيس فامتخط قيحا فمات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports differ about the afflictions that struck these men.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض ما أصاب هؤلاء اختلاف والله أعلم.

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says al-Athram or Baʿkak died of a lethal abscess, while the other died of pleurisy.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل أصاب الأثرم أو بعككا الدبيلة والآخر ذات الجنب فماتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning means the mockers will learn their recompense in the afterlife for ridiculing revelation and associating a partner with God, as they had been punished in this world.
rows.anchor: فسوف يعلمون وعيد لهم بالمجازاة على استهزائهم وجعلهم إلها مع الله في الآخرة كما جوزوا في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your breast” stands for the heart, and its distress is caused by the mockers’ spoken ridicule and attacks on revelation.
rows.anchor: وكني بالصدر عن القلب لأنه محله وجعل سبب الضيق ما يقولون وهو ما ينطقون به من الاستهزاء والطعن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to glorify God with praise answers their false claims and thanks Him for prophethood, messengership, monotheism, and other blessings; this is an act of belief and heart.
rows.anchor: ثم أمره تعالى بتنزيهه عن ما نسبوا إليه من اتخاذ الشريك معه مصحوبا بحمده والثناء على ما أسدي إليه من نعمة النبوة والرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being among those who prostrate means praying; prostration stands for prayer as the body’s noblest act and the servant’s nearest state to the Lord.
rows.anchor: والمراد والله أعلم من المصلين فكنى بالسجود عن الصلاة وهي أشرف أفعال الجسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the mockers’ wrong involved inner belief and outward speech, God commands acts answering both: inward glorification and bodily prostration, then comprehensive worship.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الصادر من المستهزئين اعتقادا وهو فعل القلب وقولا وهو ما يقولون في الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These commands mean to persist in glorification, prayer, and worship, practices the Prophet already maintained.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأوامر معناها دم على كذا لأنه صلى الله عليه وسلم ما زال متلبسا بها

rows.speaker: الجمهور وابن عمر ومجاهد والحسن وقتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: The majority, including Ibn Umar, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd, interpret certainty as death: worship should continue for as long as one lives.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن المراد باليقين الموت

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: At Uthman ibn Mazʿun’s death, the Prophet said that he had seen certainty; another transmission says certainty had come to him.
rows.anchor: قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم في عثمان بن مظعون عند موته أما هو فقد رأى اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death is not literally named “certainty”; it is called that figuratively because every rational person knows it will certainly come.
rows.anchor: وليس اليقين من أسماء الموت وإنما العلم به يقين لا يمتري فيه عاقل فسمي يقينا تجوزا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية وابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya and Ibn Bahr allow “certainty” to mean the promised victory over the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية ويحتمل أن يكون المعنى حتى يأتيك اليقين في النصر الذي وعدته انتهى وقاله ابن بحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ending the command at death ensures worship continues throughout life; without that endpoint, a single act might technically fulfill the unqualified command.
rows.anchor: وحكمة التغيية باليقين وهو الموت أنه يقتضي ديمومة العبادة ما دام حيا بخلاف الاقتصار على الأمر بالعبادة غير مغيا

none: Qur’an text only; no commentary point to record.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The transition recalls the previous oath to question all people: God’s command is the Day of Resurrection, when they will answer for their earthly crimes.
rows.anchor: ووجه ارتباطها بما قبلها أنه تعالى لما قال:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets God’s command as the Prophet’s victory and triumph over the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس المراد بالأمر:

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the unbelievers mockingly demanded the promised Hour or the punishment that would reach them at Badr.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: كانوا يستعجلون ما وعدوا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj identifies the command with the promised victory over enemies, including killing, captivity, seizure of property, and taking their homes.
rows.anchor: وهذا الثاني قاله ابن جريج قال:

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets the command as God’s ordinances and rulings; Abu Hayyan finds this remote because companions are not reported to have hastened obligations before their imposition.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الأمر هنا مصدر أمر

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن جريج
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj also take the command as God’s punishment of those who persist in idolatry and deny the Messenger; Quraysh and others often demanded that punishment hastily.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وابن جريج أيضا: الأمر عقاب الله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj gives a close interpretation: the command is the recompense God promised for their unbelief.
rows.anchor: وقريب من هذا القول قول الزجاج: هو ما وعدهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the command as one of the portents of the Hour.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأمر بعض أشراط الساعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Has arrived” can mean that the promise has arrived but its occurrence should not be hastened, that its first signs have come, or that the past tense marks a near and certain future as a threat.
rows.anchor: وأتى قيل: باق على معناه من المضي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read “do not hasten it” with second-person tā, addressing believers or, by the Prophet’s instruction, the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: تستعجلوه بالتاء

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr reads the verb with yā as a prohibition directed at the unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن جبير: بالياء نهيا للكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “do not hasten it” most naturally refers to the command just mentioned.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عود الضمير في فلا تستعجلوه على الأمر لأنه هو المحدث عنه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading takes the pronoun to refer to God: do not hasten God by demanding punishment or the Hour.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يعود على الله أي: فلا تستعجلوا الله بالعذاب،

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read “you associate” with second-person tā; the other listed readers use the third-person form, while additional readers vary the two verbs.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: تشركون بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers reading “what they associate” because their demand for punishment is mockery and denial, themselves forms of associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وأفضل قراءته عما يشركون باستعجالهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle mā may be either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وما يحتمل أن تكون بمعنى الذي ومصدرية.

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read yunazzilu with a lightened zāy; the remaining canonical readers double it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير، وأبو عمرو: ينزل مخففا

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي والأعمش وأبو بكر
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali, al-Aʿmash, and Abu Bakr read tunazzalu with a doubled zāy in the passive, with “the angels” nominative.
rows.anchor: وزيد بن علي والأعمش وأبو بكر: تنزل مشددا مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: الجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari has the same passive nominative reading but lightens the zāy.
rows.anchor: والجحدري كذلك، إلا أنه خفف.

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو العالية والأعرج والمفضل عن عاصم ويعقوب
rows.claim: Hasan, Abu al-Aliya, al-Aʿraj, al-Mufaddal from Asim, and Yaqub read the verb with open tā and doubled zāy in the active voice.
rows.anchor: والحسن، وأبو العالية، والأعرج، والمفضل، عن عاصم ويعقوب:

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Abla reads “We send down” with majestic plural nūn and doubling; Qatada uses nūn with a lightened form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة: ما ننزل بنون العظمة والتشديد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan reports Ibn ʿAtiyya’s judgment that the two nūn readings are anomalous because nearby wording has third-person pronouns.
rows.anchor: وفيهما شذوذ كثير انتهى. وشذوذهما أن ما قبله وما بعده ضمير غيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan explains the pronoun shift as rhetorical iltifāt, a change in address.
rows.anchor: ووجهه أنه التفات

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say the angel called “the spirit” here is Gabriel alone.
rows.anchor: والملائكة هنا جبريل وحده قاله الجمهور

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies the angels with those mentioned as “the rippers,” referring to 79:1.
rows.anchor: أو الملائكة المشار إليهم بقوله: والنازعات غرقا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says “the spirit” is revelation, which angels bring down to prophets; he compares the phrase about God casting the spirit to whom He wills.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الروح الوحي تنزل به الملائكة

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas says the spirit is the Qur’an, citing the revelation of a spirit from God’s command.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن أنس: هو القرآن

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the spirit means created spirits: no angel descends without a spirit accompanying him.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: المراد بالروح أرواح الخلق

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada interpret the spirit as mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة: الروح الرحمة.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes the spirit as guidance, which gives life to hearts as spirits give life to bodies.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: ما معناه الروح الهداية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the spirit as Gabriel, supported by the verse saying the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down; the preposition can be circumstantial or mean “with.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: الروح جبريل، ويدل عليه: نزل به الروح الأمين

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says the spirit is a class of guardian beings over angels, unseen to them as angels are unseen guardians over humans.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الروح حفظة على الملائكة لا تراهم الملائكة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also says the Spirit is the name of an angel, citing the day when the Spirit and angels stand in rows.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد أيضا: الروح اسم ملك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the spirit is a created being in human form that accompanies every angel descending from heaven; Ibn Jurayj gives a similar report, which Ibn ʿAtiyya calls weak for lack of transmission.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: أن الروح خلق من خلق الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari defines the spirit as revelation that revives hearts dead through ignorance, or what performs the role of a bodily spirit in religion.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: بالروح من أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From His command” can be partitive or explanatory, and “whom He wills” means the prophets.
rows.anchor: ومن للتبعيض، أو لبيان الجنس. ومن يشاء: هم الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An is a verbal noun particle governing the subjunctive and may be appositional to “the spirit,” or follow an omitted preposition, leaving a case disagreement.
rows.anchor: وأن مصدرية، وهي التي من شأنها أن تنصب المضارع،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats “that they warn” as an apposition to “the spirit,” with a lightened particle, an omitted subject pronoun, and an implied verb of saying.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وأن أنذروا بدلا من الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects that syntactic complication, saying there is no need for it when the particle can simply be the verbal-noun form that governs the subjunctive.
rows.anchor: فجعلها المخفف من الثقيلة، وأضمر اسمها وهو ضمير الشأن،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية وأبو البقاء وصاحب الغنيان
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya, Abu al-Baqā, and the author of al-Ghunyān allow an explanatory particle with no syntactic position because revelation implies speech.
rows.anchor: وجوز ابن عطية، وأبو البقاء، وصاحب الغنيان: أن تكون مفسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has “so that they warn that,” with an alternate form of the verb.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: لينذروا أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is fitting even without an explicit threat word: the audience denies God’s divinity, so the command and declaration of oneness imply rejection of idols and a warning against their worship.
rows.anchor: وحسنت النذارة هنا وإن لم يكن في اللفظ ما فيه خوف من حيث كان المنذرون كافرين بألوهيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “So fear Me” means avoid God’s punishment by taking another deity alongside Him.
rows.anchor: ومعنى: فاتقون أي اتقوا عقابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Except I” quotes the meaning rather than the exact noun: “except God” would match the preceding wording, but quoting the first-person speaker is more eloquent and underscores divine oneness.
rows.anchor: وجاءت الحكاية على المعنى في قوله: إلا أنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation of the heavens and earth proves God’s oneness because the audience admits He created them, and no other being can do so.
rows.anchor: ثم دل على وحدانيته وأنه لا إله إلا هو بما ذكر مما لا يقدر عليه غيره من خلق السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation “in truth” means in the fitting way, displaying attributes proper to a creator—life, knowledge, power, and will—which the alleged partners lack.
rows.anchor: وبالحق أي: بالواجب اللائق

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads “So exalted is God” with an additional conjunction fāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: فتعالى بزيادة فاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sentence calls attention to God’s transcendence as creator of the upper and lower worlds, beyond any partner in worship.
rows.anchor: وجاءت هذه الجملة منبهة على تنزيه الله تعالى موجد هذا العالم العلوي والعالم السفلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the external proof from cosmic creation, God gives an argument from the human being’s own creation from a sperm drop; humans should obey rather than quarrel.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر ما دل على وحدانيته من خلق العالم العلوي والأرض،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Contentious” is an intensive noun for one who disputes or a disputant, and “manifest” means either plainly contentious or one who makes contention plain.
rows.anchor: والخصيم من صفات المبالغة من خصم بمعنى اختصم، أو بمعنى مخاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context most naturally condemns humans for disputing God’s messengers with false arguments; elsewhere scripture usually presents the human being in a blameworthy setting.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن سياق هذين الوصفين سياق ذم لما تقدم من قوله: سبحانه وتعالى عما يشركون

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some identify the human being in the verse as Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالإنسان هنا أبي بن خلف الجمحي.

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others take the two descriptions as praise: God enabled a human to dispute and distinguish truth from falsehood, and elevated him from sperm to articulate speech.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: سياق الوصفين سياق المدح، لأنه تعالى قواه على منازعة الخصوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then” marks suddenness after the human’s formation, while the developmental stages between sperm and speech are left unstated.
rows.anchor: وإذ هنا للمفاجأة، وبعد خلقه من النطفة لم تقع المفاجأة بالمخاطبة

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi argues at length that humans are the noblest bodies after the celestial spheres and stars; Abu Hayyan rejects the claim that those spheres outrank humans.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: اعلم أن أشرف الأجسام بعد الأفلاك والكواكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After human creation, the passage lists livelihood blessings, beginning with livestock because they provide the greatest benefits and address the people among whom the Qur’an was revealed; livestock were discussed in al-Anʿam.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر خلق الإنسان ذكر ما امتن به عليه في قوام معيشته،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “For you in them is warmth” begins a fresh statement of livestock benefits; “warmth” is the subject, “for you” its predicate, and “in them” attaches to the locative sense of “for you.”
rows.anchor: والأظهر أن يكون لكم فيها دفء استئناف لذكر ما ينتفع بها من جهتها،

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqā allows “in them” to modify “warmth” as a circumstantial phrase, or “for you” to be circumstantial with “in them” as predicate; Abu Hayyan rejects the latter because a circumstantial phrase governed by a semantic relation cannot precede the whole clause.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو البقاء أن يكون فيها حالا من دفء، إذ لو تأخر لكان صفة.

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash allows a middle-position circumstantial phrase, whereas the majority prohibit it; all allow the circumstantial phrase after the clause.
rows.anchor: فإن تأخرت الحال عن الجملة جازت بلا خلاف، أو توسطت فأجاز ذلك الأخفش، ومنعه الجمهور.

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqā also allows “warmth” to be governed by “for you” or treated as its adjective, with the whole phrase circumstantial of the object pronoun; Abu Hayyan says this is a phrase, not a clause.
rows.anchor: وأجاز أيضا أن يرتفع دفء بلكم أو نعتها بأل، والجملة كلها حال من الضمير المنصوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says the proposed analysis is not a clause: it amounts to a single nominal phrase, “He created them for you, with warmth in them.”
rows.anchor: ولا تسمى جملة، لأن التقدير:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible parse connects “for you” to “He created them” and begins a separate statement with “in them is warmth.”
rows.anchor: وجوزوا أن يكون لكم متعلقا بخلقها، وفيها دفء استئناف لذكر منافع الأنعام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fresh-statement reading is supported by the parallel “for you in them is beauty”: warmth is a necessary benefit, beauty a nonessential one.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد كون لكم فيها دفء يظهر فيه الاستئناف مقابلته بقوله: ولكم فيها جمال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses warmth as the offspring of everything; al-Ummawi records this as a dialectal usage among some Arabs.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الدفء نسل كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Livestock” is most likely accusative by anticipation with a resumptive pronoun construction, supported by the preceding verbal clause and a rare nominative reading.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن نصب والأنعام على الاشتغال، وحسن النصب كون جملة فعلية تقدمت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري وابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyya also allow “livestock” to coordinate as an explanatory apposition, leaving “for you” independent or attached to “He created them.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري، وابن عطية: يجوز أن يكون قد عطف على البيان

rows.speaker: الزهري وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri and Abu Jaʿfar read ḍafʾ with a ḍamma and doubled fāʾ, shifting the hamza’s vowel to fāʾ and doubling it as if pausing.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري وأبو جعفر: دفء بضم الفاء وشدها وتنوينها

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads daf by transferring the vowel and deleting the hamza without doubling fāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: دف بنقل الحركة، وحذف الهمزة دون تشديد الفاء.

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiʿ describes al-Zuhri’s reading as ḍaf without hamza; some double fāʾ to compensate for the deleted hamza, including a paused reading of Hamza ibn Habib.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح: الزهري دف بضم الفاء من غير همز

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid lists livestock benefits as riding, carrying, milk, ghee, cooking over them, and other uses.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ومنافع الركوب، والحمل، والألبان، والسمن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names eating separately, just as it names warmth separately, because each is among the greatest benefits.
rows.anchor: وأفرد منفعة الأكل بالذكر، كما أفرد منفعة الدفء، لأنهما من أعظم المنافع.
